content: National authorities should consider both public and private stakeholders at central and decentralized levels who are actively engaged in gender-related issues, policymakers, civil society beneficiaries, and women’s groups, among other relevant stakeholder groups, during their stakeholder mapping exercises. This mapping process should be participatory, involving workshops, informant interviews, and consultations. Once relevant stakeholders are identified, it is beneficial to collaboratively conduct a SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) analysis to evaluate the implementation of the One Health approach. This analysis serves as a critical foundation for subsequent discussions and decision-making processes. Regional representatives may also undertake regional mapping exercises, while countries can conduct subnational stakeholder mapping as needed. It is essential for countries to review their existing One Health governance and coordination mechanisms, as these form the foundation for implementing One Health activities. Adherence to the core values and principles of good governance is crucial to achieving and sustaining the desired impact and outcomes of the One Health approach. The ultimate goal is to enhance global, regional, and national capacities to address current and future health challenges at the human-animal-plant-environment interface. Good governance is underpinned by three core principles: participation and inclusion, accountability and rule of law, and equality and non-discrimination. These principles create an enabling environment for relevant institutions and coordination mechanisms to operate effectively, adapt, and achieve their objectives. The review of governance mechanisms should encompass their types, scales, scope, and formality, as well as their strengths. The outcomes of this review will guide national-level stakeholders in strengthening or developing new sustainable, multisectoral One Health governance and coordination mechanisms. Countries should also review completed and ongoing assessments and plans related to One Health, as well as secondary data and information sources, to inform priority-setting for national One Health implementation. A comprehensive list of existing national action plans, strategies, and frameworks should be compiled. Tools for identifying completed assessments are available in the One Health and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the OHLEP inventory of resources. Some existing tools may not have been designed with a One Health framework in mind, necessitating coordination across all relevant sectors to address any gaps in scope. Engagement with United Nations Country Teams can ensure that Resident Coordinators and UN Country Teams incorporate One Health into national UNSDCFs. This integration supports the mainstreaming of One Health approaches into national development plans, highlighting the added value of One Health in managing competing priorities in country planning. Given the importance of One Health for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), it is essential to include this approach in the development of both the Common Country Analysis and the UNSDCF. Institutionalizing One Health governance requires a multisectoral coordination mechanism, such as one led by the president’s or prime minister’s office, supported by an inter-ministerial steering group. This mechanism should be backed by an adequate secretariat, technical working groups, and sufficient budget to function effectively and sustainably. For countries without such a mechanism, establishing one is a prerequisite for advancing One Health implementation planning. Resources for establishing One Health mechanisms are available in the OHLEP inventory. The national One Health committee should develop and agree upon terms of reference, with responsibilities including promoting coordination, collaboration, and communication among multisectoral stakeholders and supporting the implementation of the One Health approach. The committee should also liaise with other relevant national committees to exchange information and collaborate on One Health objectives. Regular stakeholder meetings and discussions are essential to facilitate information exchange and encourage experts from diverse fields to address cross-sectoral topics collaboratively. The committee must ensure equitable representation from all relevant sectors, including gender equity and sensitivity in governance. Following a comprehensive One Health situation analysis, national authorities, guided by the national multisectoral One Health coordination mechanism, should develop or strengthen their national One Health action plan. This plan should identify key objectives, outputs, and activities aligned with the three pathways of the One Health Joint Plan of Action (OH JPA): governance, policy, legislation, financing, and advocacy; organizational and institutional development, implementation, and sectoral integration; and technical and operational activities. Pathway 1 focuses on strengthening the enabling environment and sustainability of activities by institutionalizing intersectoral governance, providing policies and political will, enabling regulatory frameworks, and attracting equitable and sustainable investments. This pathway lays the groundwork for stakeholders to develop and implement activities at national and subnational levels while engaging with regional and international efforts. Embedding policy, legal frameworks, advocacy, and financing into the national One Health action plan ensures the sustainability of activities across all pathways. Governance involves overseeing the coordination and implementation of One Health activities through a national multisectoral coordination mechanism. Policy and legislation form the backbone of One Health governance, enabling multisectoral collaboration, coordination, and communication. National governing bodies must adapt, create, and support legislation, regulations, and procedures to establish functional multisectoral coordination mechanisms and technical working groups with clear terms of reference, budgets, and accountability frameworks. This structure facilitates routine and emergency cross-sectoral collaboration, data sharing, and joint efforts. Financing is critical for successful and sustainable One Health implementation. Costing and prioritizing action plans, mapping potential investors, and analyzing the resource environment are essential steps. Breaking siloed funding approaches and mobilizing joint investments can enhance efficiency and impact. Multisectoral coordination mechanisms should map existing and potential resources, address funding gaps, and advise on resource mobilization and allocation. Advocacy efforts are also necessary to promote the recognition and adoption of One Health, particularly among policymakers and governments. Pathway 2 focuses on organizational and institutional development, implementation, and sectoral integration. Capacity building for key personnel through joint training activities is essential to promote collaborative approaches and techniques. Training and education on One Health should be integrated into curricula at all educational levels. Staff exchanges and capacity-building opportunities for diverse groups can enhance collaboration and effectiveness. Implementation involves developing or revising operational plans that include prioritized joint activities at national and subnational levels, such as surveillance, risk assessments, outbreak response, and environmental monitoring. Sectoral integration extends beyond national coordination mechanisms to ensure collaboration across all relevant sectors. Joint communication and advocacy efforts are critical to promoting the uptake of the One Health concept and securing financing for its implementation.
